title: Good Job.
author: Jolein
summary: Jolein argues that reflexive praise—'good job,' 'nice work'—fails children and adults not because it's cruel but because it's inaccurate. Children already know who practiced and who didn't; participation trophies don't create entitlement so much as they teach that recognition and achievement are the same thing. The alternative is specific, process-focused observation: naming what the person actually did, the effort or strategy deployed, and the inner persistence shown—because this is what creates the conditions for genuine replication.
points: Children are not fooled by participation trophies: they already know who scored, who practiced, and who pulled dandelions—the trophy doesn't fool them, it conflates recognition with achievement.
Reflexive praise like 'good job' registers as social noise rather than meaningful feedback; it conveys no information about what was done or how to replicate it.

Specific process observations—naming the effort, strategy, or inner persistence behind a result—create the conditions for genuine improvement because they identify what the person actually controlled.
When a person can identify the effort or strategy behind a result, they are more likely to replicate those actions; vague praise prevents this attribution and short-circuits development.
Accurate mirrors—honest, specific, process-focused feedback—may feel less comfortable than 'good job,' but they are what people actually need in order to grow.
quotes: I noticed you kept reading even when that paragraph got confusing.” “You asked a deeper question today than yesterday.” “You changed your strategy after the first one didn’t work.” Now I’m handing them a mirror that reflects something true and that they can actually use.
Next time, I will reply “Not yet.” Tell me “good job” when I finally hold Warrior 3 on the right side for more than a few seconds or when I stop wobbling through Half Moon.
The happiest man in the universe, maybe it’s all of the exercise endorphins, always greets me with a cheerful, “good morning.” I scan my barcode.
If a person can identify the effort, the strategy, or the inner persistence, they are more likely to replicate those actions.
I remember holding mine and having a thought that I probably wasn’t supposed to have at five years old: I didn’t earn this.
